Forecasters predicting infectious disease outbreaks have met with varying success. When many forecasters each predict many different targets, is is difficult to identify why their performance varies.
We suggest a conceptual framework for identifying factors that contribute to forecast performance. We separate the process of creating a forecast from the processes that create the forecasting target in question. We identify common strategies for addressing this challenge, and demonstrate a regression-based approach to evaluation with sparse data.

We evaluated forecasts of weekly COVID-19 cases and deaths over two years across 32 European countries, scored against observed data with the weighted interval score (WIS).
We classified 48 models by structure (agent-based, mechanistic, semi-mechanistic, statistical, or human judgement) and estimated how much structure alone affected performance.
A generalised additive mixed model adjusted for what makes a target easier or harder to predict: the outcome being forecast, its level and trend, the dominant variant, the country, the forecast horizon, and differences between individual models.

Once we accounted for the difficulty of the target, no single type of model performed best.
That average concealed structures which predicted one outcome relatively well and the other relatively poorly, differences that cancelled when averaged across case and death forecasts.
Performance was driven more by which targets were hard to predict than by which modelling approach a forecaster used.

This approach sits between informal and fully formal ways of handling bias in evaluation studies.
As infectious disease forecasting grows, we encourage evaluators to choose from a wider range of study designs, matching the formality of the method to the question and data available.
Specifically, evaluating across multiple forecast targets requires explicit accounting for the variation producing each target, before considering what varies within the forecasting process.
